readerTitle: Why Enterprise opened its offices next to repair shops, not airports
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Enterprise Rent-A-Car) + 포지셔닝 개념 출처 (Ries & Trout) + 가상 적용 (IT 지원 회사, 배관 업체)
insight: 포지셔닝은 광고 문구가 아니라 '누구에게, 무엇 대신 선택되는가'를 정하는 일이다. 정하지 않아도 고객은 이미 당신을 어딘가에 분류해 두고 있다.
misconception: 모두에게 어필해야 시장이 커진다. 포지셔닝은 슬로건을 만드는 마케팅 부서의 일이다.

sources.text: Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1981). Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. McGraw-Hill.
Enterprise Holdings, company history (founding in St. Louis, 1957; home-city replacement rentals; "We'll pick you up")

factChecks.note: Enterprise는 1957년 Jack Taylor가 St. Louis에서 리스 회사(Executive Leasing)로 시작했고 이후 렌터카 사업을 했다는 내용을 Enterprise Holdings 공식 연혁으로 확인하세요.
수리·사고로 차를 쓸 수 없는 지역 고객(home-city, insurance replacement)에 집중하고 보험사·정비소와 협력했다는 점, 공항 진출은 나중(1990년대 중반)이라는 점을 공식 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도 없이 "only later"로만 적었습니다.
"We'll pick you up" 슬로건과 픽업 서비스가 Enterprise의 대표 특징이라는 점을 확인하세요. 규모는 수치 없이 "one of the largest rental companies in the US"로만 적었습니다.
포지셔닝 개념은 Ries & Trout가 1969·1972년 기고문과 1981년 책으로 대중화했습니다. 카드에는 1981년 책만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: Why Enterprise opened its offices next to repair shops, not airports
body: For decades, the big car rental brands fought over the same ground: airport counters and business travelers.
One company grew into a giant by mostly staying out of that fight. It went where people's cars broke down.

image.label: A small rental office beside a car repair shop, far from an airport
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽 멀리 공항 렌터카 카운터들이 붐비고, 오른쪽 가까이에 동네 정비소 옆 작은 렌터카 사무실. 직원이 고객을 차로 태우러 가는 모습. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your IT support firm sounds like everyone else.
body: You run a 12-person IT support firm. Your website says "IT solutions for every business." You compete with big national providers and cheap freelancers.
Leads are few, and most just compare prices. What do you change first?

options.text: List more services so no buyer feels left out
options.feedback: You cover more ground on paper, but you look even more like everyone else. A longer list rarely gives a buyer a reason to pick you.

options.text: Pick one type of client, like medical clinics that can't afford downtime, and build your offer around them
options.feedback: You give up some general leads, but the clients you pick now see a firm made for them. That's the idea in this lesson.

options.text: Cut prices below the big providers
options.feedback: It may win deals quickly. But "the cheaper one" is a spot bigger rivals and freelancers can take from you any time.

cards.title: The customer the big brands ignored.
body: Enterprise started in St. Louis in 1957 as a car leasing business. Its rental side aimed at someone the airport brands mostly overlooked: a person at home whose car was in the shop.
So it opened small offices in neighborhoods, worked with insurance companies and repair shops that sent it customers, and became known for one promise: **"We'll pick you up."**
It grew into one of the largest rental companies in the US, and only later expanded into airports.

cards.title: Positioning
body: **Positioning** is the place your business holds in a customer's mind, compared with the other options they'd consider.

Al Ries and Jack Trout made the idea popular in their 1981 book *Positioning*. Their point: the fight isn't only in the market. It's in the customer's head, where each business gets filed under a simple label.
Enterprise's label was clear: the rental company for when your own car is out of action.

image.label: A customer's mind with businesses filed into labeled slots
image.brief: 사람 머리 실루엣 안에 서랍장. 서랍마다 라벨: "Airport rentals", "Cheap option", "When my car is in the shop". 마지막 서랍에만 작은 차 아이콘이 들어 있고 강조 색. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A clear position answers three questions.
body: Enterprise's answers were short and specific:
list: **Who is it for?** People whose car is being repaired or replaced
**What would they use instead?** A lift from friends, a taxi, or a far-off airport counter
**Why choose you?** Nearby, and they come and get you
cards.callout: Vague answers to any of the three leave customers to guess.
cards.softwareNote: Software shows the same pattern. "Project management for everyone" competes with giants. "Job scheduling for small roofing crews" tells a buyer instantly whether the product is meant for them.

cards.title: You already have a position, chosen or not.
body: Customers file every business somewhere: "the pricey one," "the one my neighbor uses," "no idea what they do." If you don't choose a spot, they choose one for you, and it's usually vague.

A chosen position also drives real decisions. Enterprise's office locations, its insurance partners and its pick-up service all followed from who it served. Positioning is a strategy choice, not just a slogan.

image.label: Office map, partners and pick-up van all pointing to one customer
image.brief: 가운데 "Car in the shop" 고객 아이콘. 주변의 "Neighborhood offices", "Insurance partners", "Pick-up service" 아이콘이 모두 화살표로 고객을 향함. 깔끔한 인포그래픽, 로고 없음.

cards.title: A clear spot has a price.
body: Choosing a position means some customers will pass you by. That's the trade. The spot also has to be big enough to support the business.
And saying it doesn't make it true. A position only holds if what you deliver matches it, every time.
Markets also move. A spot that works today may need to be revisited, as Enterprise did when it later chose to compete at airports.

cards.title: Now it's a plumbing business.
body: Ten plumbers in your city all advertise "fast, reliable, affordable." You notice many of your calls come from landlords with several rental units, who hate chasing tenants to arrange access.
How do you position your business?

options.text: Keep "fast, reliable, affordable" and buy more ads
options.feedback: More ads make you more visible, but you'd be paying to say what ten rivals already say. Customers still have no reason to remember you.

options.text: Become "the plumber for rental owners": you book with tenants directly and send photo reports
options.feedback: You may lose some homeowner calls, but landlords get a clear reason to choose you and to call back. The service changes, not just the slogan.

options.text: Raise prices and call yourselves "premium plumbers"
options.feedback: It sets you apart, but it doesn't say who you're for or what makes the extra cost worth it. Premium for whom?

cards.title: Choose the spot you want in your customer's mind.
body: Positioning means deciding who you're for, what they'd use instead, and why they should pick you, then building the business to match.
**Try it today:** ask three recent customers how they'd describe you to a friend. Compare their words with the spot you want to own.
